form.title: Cambridge Lower Secondary Stage 9 onboarding test

writes.rule: Per subtopic seen: pMastery 0.7 if right at D2/D3, 0.55 if right at D1, 0.25 if wrong; level L0-L3 from the ladder step reached
Prerequisite-gap index = 100 x weighted misses / weighted items seen in slots 1-4, averaged over groups
Groups with the highest Part A percent (top 1-2, only if >= 65%)
Groups with the lowest Part A percent (bottom 1-2, only if < 65%)
Calibration = 1 - mean |confidence/5 - correct| over Part A (feeds the first MCI reading)
Highest difficulty answered correctly twice in a row: D1 low, D2 medium, D3 high
Verbal reasoning = percent of Part B verbal items right
Numerical reasoning = percent of Part B numerical items right
Abstract reasoning = percent of Part B abstract items right
Spatial reasoning = percent of Part B spatial items right
Logical deduction = percent right on Part B items tagged p65
Numeracy fluency = numerical percent scaled by speed (right answers under target time count 1.2x, max 100)
Processing speed = 100 x share of Part B items answered right within target seconds
RIASEC profile: each career-interest item scored 1-5; letter score = mean of its 2 items; top 3 letters form the code (e.g. IRC)

items.stem: Which of these numbers is a perfect square?
items.markingKey: C. 196. 14 x 14 = 196; the others are not the square of any whole number
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: multiplication facts and squares of numbers

items.stem: Which shows 36 written as a product of prime factors?
items.markingKey: A. 2 x 2 x 3 x 3. 4, 6 and 9 are not prime; 36 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 6-7: factors, primes and prime factorisation

items.stem: The prime factorisation of 180 is
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 6-7: factors, primes and prime factorisation

items.stem: 5⁴ means
items.markingKey: C. 5 x 5 x 5 x 5. The exponent 4 says how many 5s are multiplied
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: exponents and powers

items.stem: What is the value of 2⁵?
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: exponents and powers

items.stem: Which is greater, 3⁴ or 4³, and by how much?
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: exponents and powers

items.markingKey: C. -3. Start at -8 and move 5 to the right on the number line
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: integers and fractions, four operations

items.markingKey: C. 1/12. Common denominator 12: 9/12 - 8/12 = 1/12
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: integers and fractions, four operations

items.stem: A jug holds 2 1/2 litres of milk. 3/4 litre is used for tea and 1 1/3 litres for a pudding. How much milk is left?
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: integers and fractions, four operations

items.stem: Which of these numbers is irrational?
items.markingKey: C. √2. √49 = 7; only √2 cannot be written as a fraction

items.stem: Which statement is true?
items.markingKey: B. √12 lies between 3 and 4. 3² = 9 and 4² = 16, and 12 is between them

items.stem: Which of these products is a rational number?
Write 45 000 in standard form.
items.markingKey: B. 4.5 x 10⁴. Standard form is A x 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10

items.stem: Write 0.000 36 in standard form.
items.markingKey: D. 3.6 x 10⁻⁴. Move the decimal point 4 places to the right

items.stem: Work out (3 x 10⁵) x (4 x 10³). Give your answer in standard form.
Write the value of 7⁰.
items.markingKey: C. 1. Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1

items.stem: Write 2⁻³ as a fraction.
Simplify (x⁴)³ ÷ x⁵.
items.markingKey: D. x⁷. (x⁴)³ = x¹²; x¹² ÷ x⁵ = x⁷

items.stem: Expand 3(x + 4).
items.subtopicHint: Expanding the product of two linear expressions
items.markingKey: D. 3x + 12. Multiply both terms by 3

items.stem: Expand and simplify (x + 3)(x + 5).
items.subtopicHint: Expanding the product of two linear expressions

items.stem: Expand and simplify (2x - 3)(x + 4).
items.subtopicHint: Expanding the product of two linear expressions

items.stem: A potted plant is kept in a dark cupboard for 3 days. One leaf is then tested with iodine. What do you expect, and why?
items.answer: No blue-black colour, because no starch was made without light
options: No blue-black colour, because iodine reacts only with sugar
No blue-black colour, because no starch was made without light
Blue-black colour, because the plant made starch from soil water
Blue-black colour, because leaves always store starch
items.markingKey: B. No blue-black colour, because no starch was made without light. Iodine turns blue-black with starch; without light the plant uses up its starch and cannot make more
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: nutrition in plants (photosynthesis)

items.stem: In a circuit diagram, a long line drawn next to a short line stands for
items.markingKey: D. A cell. The long line is the positive terminal of a cell
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: electric circuits and their components

items.stem: A bulb does not glow when a rubber eraser closes the gap in a circuit, but glows with a steel key. This shows that
items.answer: steel is a conductor and rubber is an insulator
options: steel is a conductor and rubber is an insulator
both are conductors but rubber is weaker
rubber is a conductor and steel is an insulator
items.markingKey: A. steel is a conductor and rubber is an insulator. Current flows through conductors such as metals, not through insulators such as rubber
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: electric circuits and their components

items.stem: In an experiment, the factor you deliberately change is called the
items.markingKey: D. independent variable. You change the independent variable and measure the dependent one
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: planning a fair investigation

items.stem: A student wants to test whether salt makes ice melt faster. What must stay the same in both cups?
items.answer: The size of the ice cubes and the room temperature
options: Only the time she checks the result
The size of the ice cubes and the room temperature
items.markingKey: C. The size of the ice cubes and the room temperature. Only one factor (salt) should change; everything else is controlled
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: planning a fair investigation

items.stem: A student says plants grow taller with music. He plays music to one plant on a sunny window and keeps another plant, without music, in a dark corner. What is wrong with his test?
items.answer: Two factors (music and light) changed, so he cannot tell which caused the difference
options: He should have used three plants with music
Two factors (music and light) changed, so he cannot tell which caused the difference
Plants cannot hear, so no test is needed
He should measure the leaves, not the height
items.markingKey: B. Two factors (music and light) changed, so he cannot tell which caused the difference. A fair test changes one variable at a time
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: planning a fair investigation

items.stem: Digestion of starch begins in the
items.markingKey: C. mouth. Saliva contains an enzyme that starts breaking starch down
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: nutrition in animals (human digestive system)

items.stem: Why is the inner wall of the small intestine covered with finger-like villi?
items.answer: They increase the surface area for absorbing digested food
options: They increase the surface area for absorbing digested food
They push food back to the stomach
items.markingKey: A. They increase the surface area for absorbing digested food. More surface means faster absorption into the blood
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: nutrition in animals (human digestive system)

items.stem: A person whose gall bladder was removed is advised to eat less oily food. Which reason fits best?
items.answer: Bile, which breaks fat into small droplets, is no longer stored and released in large amounts
options: The stomach can no longer make acid
Fat is digested only in the gall bladder
Bile, which breaks fat into small droplets, is no longer stored and released in large amounts
items.markingKey: C. Bile, which breaks fat into small droplets, is no longer stored and released in large amounts. The gall bladder stores bile; without it less bile is available at mealtimes to emulsify fat
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: nutrition in animals (human digestive system)

items.stem: Which word equation represents photosynthesis?
items.markingKey: A. carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Light energy turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen

items.stem: Why do greenhouse plants often grow faster when extra carbon dioxide is added to the air?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so more glucose can be made
options: Carbon dioxide gives plants energy directly
Plants absorb carbon dioxide through their roots
Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so more glucose can be made
items.markingKey: C. Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so more glucose can be made. More raw material raises the rate when carbon dioxide is the limiting factor

items.stem: Pondweed gives off 12 bubbles per minute with a lamp 10 cm away and 4 bubbles per minute with the lamp 40 cm away. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.answer: The rate of photosynthesis falls as light intensity falls
options: Temperature has no effect on photosynthesis
The rate of photosynthesis falls as light intensity falls
Pondweed photosynthesises only when the lamp is at 10 cm
items.markingKey: C. The rate of photosynthesis falls as light intensity falls. Moving the lamp away lowers light intensity; fewer oxygen bubbles means a lower rate

items.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
items.markingKey: A. photosynthesis. The other three release carbon dioxide

items.stem: Fossil fuels contain carbon because
items.answer: they formed from the remains of organisms that took in carbon millions of years ago
options: carbon dioxide soaks into rocks every day
they are made in factories from carbon
they formed from the remains of organisms that took in carbon millions of years ago
they absorb carbon from the air when burned
items.markingKey: C. they formed from the remains of organisms that took in carbon millions of years ago. Coal, oil and gas are ancient plant and plankton remains

items.stem: Large areas of forest are cut down and burned. What happens to the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, and why?
items.answer: It rises: burning releases carbon dioxide and fewer trees are left to absorb it
options: It falls, because ash absorbs carbon dioxide
It stays the same, because grass replaces the trees at once
It rises: burning releases carbon dioxide and fewer trees are left to absorb it
It rises only because animals respire more
items.markingKey: C. It rises: burning releases carbon dioxide and fewer trees are left to absorb it. Two effects add up: more released, less removed

items.stem: Which particle in an atom has a negative charge?
items.subtopicHint: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table
items.markingKey: C. electron. Protons are positive, neutrons neutral

items.stem: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. How many electrons does the neutral atom have?
items.subtopicHint: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table
items.markingKey: B. 11. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons

items.stem: Elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have similar chemical properties because
items.answer: they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell
items.subtopicHint: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table
options: they have the same number of neutrons
they were discovered at the same time
they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell
items.markingKey: D. they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. Outer-shell electrons decide how an element reacts

items.stem: Density is calculated as
items.markingKey: B. mass ÷ volume. ρ = m / V

items.stem: A block has a mass of 240 g and a volume of 80 cm³. What is its density?
A solid has a density of 0.8 g/cm³; water has a density of 1.0 g/cm³. What happens when the solid is put in water, and why?
items.answer: It floats, because it is less dense than water
options: It sinks, because it is less dense than water
It floats, because it is heavier than water
It floats, because it is less dense than water
It sinks, because density does not affect floating
items.markingKey: C. It floats, because it is less dense than water. Objects less dense than a liquid float in it

items.stem: Read: 'The old fort looked desolate; no one had visited it in years.' What does 'desolate' most likely mean?
items.markingKey: A. empty and lonely. 'No one had visited it in years' signals emptiness
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: working out word meaning from context

items.stem: Choose the correct word: Yesterday, Kabir ___ his bicycle to school.
items.markingKey: A. rode. 'Yesterday' needs the simple past
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: simple past and past continuous

items.stem: Choose the correct words: When the lights went out, we ___ dinner.
items.markingKey: A. were having. An action in progress in the past uses the past continuous
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: simple past and past continuous

items.stem: Choose the correct word: Each of the students ___ a library card.
items.markingKey: C. has. 'Each' is singular
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: subject-verb agreement

items.stem: Choose the correct word: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ aware of the change.
items.markingKey: C. were. With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students'
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: subject-verb agreement

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?
items.answer: The bunch of keys was found under the sofa.
options: The bunch of keys was found under the sofa.
The bunch of keys were found under the sofa.
The bunch of keys are find under the sofa.
The bunch of keys have found under the sofa.
items.markingKey: A. The bunch of keys was found under the sofa.. The subject is 'bunch' (singular), not 'keys'
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: subject-verb agreement

items.stem: Read: "Bees visit flowers to collect nectar. As they move, pollen sticks to their bodies and is carried to other flowers. This helps plants make seeds." What is the passage mainly about?
items.answer: How bees help plants make seeds
options: How bees help plants make seeds
items.markingKey: A. How bees help plants make seeds. Every sentence builds towards pollination and seeds
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: reading for the main idea

items.stem: Read: "Arun practised the flute every evening, even when his friends called him out to play. At the school concert, the audience stood up and clapped for a long time." What is the main message?
options: Playing outside is a waste of time
items.markingKey: C. Steady practice leads to success. The practice in the first sentence explains the applause in the second
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: reading for the main idea

items.stem: Read: "Many cities now have car-free Sundays. Streets fill with cyclists, skaters and families. Shopkeepers first complained, but many now report more customers on foot." Which statement best sums up the passage?
items.answer: Car-free days, though doubted at first, benefit people and some businesses
options: Car-free days, though doubted at first, benefit people and some businesses
items.markingKey: C. Car-free days, though doubted at first, benefit people and some businesses. The summary must include both the early doubt and the later benefit
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: reading for the main idea

items.stem: 'I opened the door slowly and saw that the room was empty.' This sentence is written in the
items.markingKey: A. first person. The narrator uses 'I'

items.stem: Why might a writer tell a mystery story in the first person?
items.answer: The reader only knows what the narrator knows, which builds suspense
options: First person is always more formal
The reader only knows what the narrator knows, which builds suspense
items.markingKey: C. The reader only knows what the narrator knows, which builds suspense. Limited knowledge keeps the reader guessing

items.stem: Read: 'Marcus said he was fine. His hands, however, would not stop shaking.' What does the writer suggest by putting these sentences together?
items.answer: Marcus is hiding how anxious he really is
options: Marcus is lying about his name
Marcus is excited about good news
Marcus is hiding how anxious he really is
items.markingKey: D. Marcus is hiding how anxious he really is. 'However' signals that his body contradicts his words

items.stem: In 'The thunder growled over the hills', which word creates the strongest sense of threat?
items.markingKey: A. growled. 'Growled' makes the thunder sound like a dangerous animal

items.stem: Read: 'The corridor stretched on, endless and silent.' What effect do the words 'endless and silent' create?
items.answer: A feeling of isolation and unease
options: A feeling of isolation and unease
items.markingKey: B. A feeling of isolation and unease. No end and no sound make the place feel empty and eerie

items.stem: A writer uses very short sentences in a chase scene: 'He ran. Faster. The gate. Locked.' Why?
items.answer: To build pace and tension that mirror the character's panic
options: Because the writer ran out of words
To make the scene more formal
To build pace and tension that mirror the character's panic
items.markingKey: C. To build pace and tension that mirror the character's panic. Short, broken sentences speed up reading and feel breathless

items.stem: Which sentence is a fact?
items.answer: The museum opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays.
options: The museum's cafe serves the best coffee.
The museum opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays.
The museum is the most exciting place in the city.
items.markingKey: C. The museum opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays.. A fact can be checked

items.stem: An advert says: 'Join thousands of happy customers who already love SparkClean!' Which persuasive technique is this?
items.markingKey: C. Appeal to popularity (bandwagon). It suggests you should buy it because many others do

items.stem: A leaflet about a planned park includes only residents' positive comments and no costs. What should a careful reader conclude?
items.answer: The leaflet is one-sided, so more evidence is needed before judging
options: The leaflet is a news report
The leaflet is one-sided, so more evidence is needed before judging
items.markingKey: C. The leaflet is one-sided, so more evidence is needed before judging. Missing costs and opposing views signal bias

items.stem: 'The stars were diamonds scattered on velvet' is an example of
items.markingKey: D. a metaphor. The stars are said to BE diamonds, without 'like' or 'as'

items.stem: Which line uses onomatopoeia?
items.answer: The bees buzzed among the roses.
options: The bees buzzed among the roses.
The roses were as red as blood.
items.markingKey: B. The bees buzzed among the roses.. 'Buzzed' imitates the sound it describes

items.stem: A poem describes a city at night as 'a sleeping giant, breathing slow'. What impression is created?
items.answer: The city seems huge, calm and alive even while quiet
options: The city is dangerous and violent
The city is small and empty
The city seems huge, calm and alive even while quiet
items.markingKey: D. The city seems huge, calm and alive even while quiet. A giant suggests size; sleeping and breathing suggest calm life

items.stem: On a map with a scale of 1 : 50 000, two towns are 4 cm apart. What is the real distance between them?
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: map scale, grid references and distance

items.stem: A century is a period of
items.markingKey: C. 100 years. Centuries are 100-year periods
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: chronology, centuries and timelines

items.stem: Which order is correct, earliest first?
items.answer: Building of the Egyptian pyramids, the Roman Empire, the Industrial Revolution, the First World War
options: The Roman Empire, the Egyptian pyramids, the First World War, the Industrial Revolution
The Industrial Revolution, the Roman Empire, the Egyptian pyramids, the First World War
Building of the Egyptian pyramids, the Roman Empire, the Industrial Revolution, the First World War
The Egyptian pyramids, the Industrial Revolution, the Roman Empire, the First World War
items.markingKey: C. Building of the Egyptian pyramids, the Roman Empire, the Industrial Revolution, the First World War. About 2500 BCE, about 27 BCE to 476 CE, about 1760 to 1840, 1914 to 1918
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: chronology, centuries and timelines

items.stem: Which is a primary source about the First World War?
options: A website summary of the war
items.markingKey: D. A soldier's letter written in 1916. A primary source was made at the time by someone involved
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: using sources as evidence

items.stem: Why might a wartime newspaper be an unreliable source about the enemy country?
items.answer: It may be biased to support its own side
options: It may be biased to support its own side
It was printed on old paper
items.markingKey: A. It may be biased to support its own side. Wartime papers were often censored or used for propaganda
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: using sources as evidence

items.stem: Two historians disagree about why an empire collapsed. What is the best explanation?
items.answer: They use different evidence and give different weight to each cause
options: They use different evidence and give different weight to each cause
Empires collapse for only one reason
One of them must be lying
items.markingKey: A. They use different evidence and give different weight to each cause. Interpretations differ because evidence is selected and weighed differently
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: using sources as evidence

items.stem: Which of these is a basic human need?
items.markingKey: D. Clean water. Needs are essential for survival; the others are wants
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: human needs and why settlements grow where they do

items.stem: Why have many large cities grown up next to rivers or coasts?
items.answer: For water supply, transport and trade
options: It is cheaper to build on water
For water supply, transport and trade
items.markingKey: C. For water supply, transport and trade. Water routes carried goods and people
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: human needs and why settlements grow where they do

items.stem: A country has an ageing population. Which challenge is it most likely to face?
items.answer: More spending on pensions and healthcare, with fewer people of working age
options: More spending on pensions and healthcare, with fewer people of working age
items.markingKey: D. More spending on pensions and healthcare, with fewer people of working age. Older people need more care while the workforce shrinks
items.prerequisiteNote: Grade 7: human needs and why settlements grow where they do

items.stem: The Industrial Revolution began in the 18th century in
items.subtopicHint: History: the Industrial Revolution, causes and consequences
items.markingKey: A. Britain. Coal, capital, colonies and inventions came together in Britain first

items.stem: Which was a major consequence of the Industrial Revolution?
items.answer: Rapid growth of towns as people moved to work in factories
items.subtopicHint: History: the Industrial Revolution, causes and consequences
options: Rapid growth of towns as people moved to work in factories
items.markingKey: C. Rapid growth of towns as people moved to work in factories. Factory work drew people from the countryside

items.stem: Why did child labour in factories become common in the early 1800s?
items.answer: Children could be paid less and many families needed the income
items.subtopicHint: History: the Industrial Revolution, causes and consequences
options: Children could be paid less and many families needed the income
items.markingKey: C. Children could be paid less and many families needed the income. Low wages and poverty drove it until factory laws were passed

items.stem: Climate means
items.answer: the average weather of a place over a long period
options: the average weather of a place over a long period
items.markingKey: A. the average weather of a place over a long period. Climate is usually averaged over about 30 years

items.stem: Why are places near the Equator generally hotter than places near the poles?
items.answer: The Sun's rays are more concentrated there
options: They are much closer to the Sun
The Sun's rays are more concentrated there
items.markingKey: C. The Sun's rays are more concentrated there. Near the Equator the Sun is high, so its energy falls on a smaller area

items.stem: Coastal cities often have milder winters than inland cities at the same latitude. Why?
items.answer: The sea heats and cools more slowly than land, so it keeps coastal temperatures moderate
options: The sea heats and cools more slowly than land, so it keeps coastal temperatures moderate
Inland areas are closer to the poles
items.markingKey: A. The sea heats and cools more slowly than land, so it keeps coastal temperatures moderate. Water has a high heat capacity

items.stem: Population density means
items.answer: the number of people per square kilometre
options: the number of people per square kilometre
the total population of a country
items.markingKey: A. the number of people per square kilometre. Density = people ÷ area

items.stem: Which factor most often pushes people to move from rural areas to cities?
items.answer: Lack of jobs and services in the countryside
options: A lower cost of living in cities
Lack of jobs and services in the countryside
items.markingKey: C. Lack of jobs and services in the countryside. Push factors drive people away; jobs in cities pull them in

items.stem: A country has a birth rate of 30 per 1000 and a death rate of 10 per 1000. What is its natural increase?
items.markingKey: A. 20 per 1000 (2% a year). Birth rate minus death rate

items.stem: The United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in
items.markingKey: D. 1948. It was adopted on 10 December 1948

items.stem: Which is a responsibility that comes with the right to free speech?
items.answer: Not spreading lies that harm others
options: Not spreading lies that harm others
items.markingKey: A. Not spreading lies that harm others. Rights are limited where they harm the rights of others

items.stem: A town must choose between building a road through a forest and keeping the forest. Which approach best balances different perspectives?
items.answer: Consult residents, businesses and environmental experts, then weigh the costs and benefits
options: Consult residents, businesses and environmental experts, then weigh the costs and benefits
items.markingKey: B. Consult residents, businesses and environmental experts, then weigh the costs and benefits. Good decisions consider several stakeholders and the evidence

items.stem: What number comes next? 3, 7, 11, 15, ?
If 4 identical notebooks cost 96, what do 7 notebooks cost at the same rate?
25% of 80 is the same as 50% of which number?
What number comes next? 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
Book is to reading as fork is to ...
items.explanation: A book is used for reading; a fork is used for eating

items.stem: Which word does not belong with the others? apple, mango, carrot, banana
items.explanation: Carrot is a vegetable; the others are fruits

items.stem: All squares are rectangles. All rectangles have four sides. Which statement must be true?
options: Some rectangles do not have four sides
items.explanation: If every square is a rectangle and every rectangle has four sides, every square has four sides

items.stem: Asha is taller than Ben. Ben is taller than Chitra. Dev is shorter than Chitra. Who is the shortest?
The shapes repeat in a pattern: circle, square, triangle, circle, square, ? Which shape comes next?
items.explanation: The three shapes repeat in the same order

items.stem: Figure 1 has 1 black dot, figure 2 has 2 white dots, figure 3 has 3 black dots, figure 4 has 4 white dots. What is figure 5?
items.explanation: One more dot each time; colours alternate

items.stem: Which letter comes next? A, C, F, J, O, ?
items.explanation: The gaps grow by one: +2, +3, +4, +5, then +6

items.stem: Rule: the third figure keeps the lines that appear in only one of the first two figures and drops lines they share. A vertical line '|' and a horizontal line '-' give a cross '+'. If figure 1 is a cross '+' and figure 2 is a vertical line '|', what is figure 3?
items.explanation: The vertical line is shared, so it is dropped; the horizontal line stays

items.stem: A square sheet of paper is folded in half once along a diagonal. What shape do you get?
items.explanation: The diagonal fold puts one corner on the opposite corner

items.stem: A mirror is held upright beside each capital letter. Which letter looks the same in the mirror?
items.explanation: A has a vertical line of symmetry

items.stem: A cube is painted on all faces and cut into 27 equal small cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
items.explanation: Those are the middle cubes of the 12 edges

items.stem: You face north. You turn 90° clockwise, then 180°, then 90° anticlockwise. Which way do you face now?

items.prompt: On a normal school day, how long do you study at home (not counting tuition)?
When do you usually study best?
How long is a typical study session before you take a break?
How often do you revise topics you have already finished?
How do you usually revise?

options.label: Testing myself with flashcards or quizzes

items.prompt: I put off starting homework until the last minute.
Where is your phone while you study?

options.label: With me, I check it often

items.prompt: Which helps you learn a new topic most?
Do you prefer studying alone or with others?
When you get stuck on a question, what do you usually do first?

options.label: Search online or watch a video

items.prompt: Do you go to tuition or coaching classes?

options.label: Yes, for two or more subjects

items.prompt: I mostly study because ...

options.label: I have a goal I want to reach

items.prompt: If I work hard, I can get much better at a subject I find difficult.
I like hard problems, even when I might get them wrong.
Before a test, how nervous do you usually feel?
items.helpText: Optional. This only helps us pace your plan and suggest support; it never affects your scores or recommendations.

items.prompt: On school nights, how many hours do you usually sleep?
items.helpText: Optional. Used only to fit your timetable around enough rest.

items.prompt: How much would you enjoy this? Fixing or building things, like a bicycle, a model or a small circuit
How much would you enjoy this? Working outdoors with tools, plants or animals
How much would you enjoy this? Doing experiments to find out why something happens
